name: Guardrails for the Youngest Learners
title: Guardrails for the Youngest Learners
answer: In preschool through second grade, three guardrails carry special force: cameras should not be used to recognize or track young children, speech tools should not store recordings after a session ends, and every device a young child uses should run in its most protective child mode. These rules matter because children this age cannot understand or agree to the data being collected about them. They are simple to state and belong in every early childhood program's written policy.

sections.body: Some rules apply with more weight in the early grades than anywhere else, because the children involved cannot understand or consent to how information about them is gathered. Tools that watch a child's face or movement to judge attention, emotion or behavior collect sensitive data about a person too young to have a say. Speech tools raise a related problem, since they need to hear a child to be useful but have no reason to keep that audio afterward. The response is a short set of guardrails an early childhood program can write into policy: no camera based tracking, no stored voice, and locked down devices. Teachers can still follow behavior patterns the old way, through their own notes, with names removed before any AI tool is involved.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text addresses preschool through second grade. In those years, behavior patterns are tracked through the teacher's own notes rather than through cameras, and names come off before any AI tool touches those notes. A speech tool may listen while a child is working so that it can help, but it should not keep the recording once the session ends unless a family has agreed and there is a clear reason to keep it. Tablets and laptops used by young children should have their most protective settings turned on, with web access limited and AI features confined to tools the district has approved. Districts should also ask every speech tool vendor how long recordings are kept and who is able to hear them. Figure 5.6 gathers these guardrails in one place.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers one concrete example rather than a body of research. It points to New Mexico's decision to let districts opt out of voice recordings in a statewide AI reading test, cited as GovTech, 2026, as showing that the concern about stored audio is real. Beyond that example, the guardrails rest on practice and on the judgment of the adults who set policy, not on studies reported in this text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The guardrails are themselves the limits: cameras should not recognize or track young children, recordings should not be stored without family agreement and a clear reason, and devices should run in child mode with restricted web access and only district approved AI tools. The decisions stay with people. A family has to agree before any recording is kept, and someone in the district has to be able to state a clear reason for keeping it. Districts decide which AI tools are approved for young children, and staff carry the job of asking vendors how long recordings are kept and who can hear them. Teachers keep the judgment about behavior, recording it in their own notes with names removed. These rules are simple to state, and they deserve a place in every early childhood program's written policy.
